facts.statement: Vivaron lived during the Late Triassic (middle Norian) in the Chinle Formation of New Mexico.
facts.quote: Vivaron is a genus of rauisuchid known from the Late Triassic (middle Norian) Chinle Formation in New Mexico.

facts.statement: The genus was named in 2016 based on fossils collected at Hayden Quarry in 2009.
facts.quote: Vivaron was named in 2016 from material collected at the Hayden Quarry at Ghost Ranch, New Mexico in 2009.

facts.statement: Before Vivaron was described, all Late Triassic rauisuchid fossils from Texas, Arizona, and New Mexico were assigned to Postosuchus kirkpatricki.
facts.quote: Prior to its description, all Late Triassic rauisuchid material from Texas, Arizona and New Mexico had been referred to Postosuchus kirkpatricki.

facts.statement: The species name honors John Hayden, the hiker who discovered the quarry in 2002.
facts.quote: the specific name in honour of John Hayden, a hiker who discovered the Hayden Quarry in 2002 where the material for Vivaron was collected.

facts.statement: Estimates based on related taxa suggest Vivaron grew to between 12 and 18 feet in length.
facts.quote: Comparisons with related taxa allow for an estimated length of between 12 and 18 ft, similar in size and appearance to other rauisuchids.

facts.statement: It can be distinguished by two prongs on the posterior part of the maxilla where it meets the jugal bone.
facts.quote: Vivaron can be distinguished from other rauisuchids by the presence of two prongs on the posterior portion of the maxilla where it articulates with the jugal.

facts.statement: Fossils consist only of three jaw bones, associated skull fragments, and referred pelvic bones.
facts.quote: Vivaron es conocido solo a partir de tres huesos del hocico, fragmentos asociados del cráneo y huesos pélvicos referidos.

facts.statement: Comparisons with related taxa estimate a length of approximately 3.5 to 5 meters, similar to other rauisuchids.
facts.quote: Las comparaciones con taxones relacionados permiten estimar una longitud de ~3.5 a ~5 metros, similar en tamaño y apariencia a otros rauisúquidos.

facts.statement: It is distinguished from other rauisuchids by two projections on the posterior part of the maxilla where it articulates with the jugal.
facts.quote: Vivaron puede ser distinguido de otros rauisúquidos por la presencia de dos salientes en la parte posterior del maxilar en donde se articula con el yugal.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Postosuchus also possessed a fifth alveolus, as a reconstruction by Long and Murry (1995) possibly shows one on the left premaxilla.
facts.quote: (sin embargo, una reconstrucción de un cráneo de Postosuchus (UCMP A269) ilustrada en Long y Murry 1995 (Fig. 121) posiblemente muestra un quinto alvéolo en el premaxilar izquierdo).

facts.statement: Vivaron is classified as a member of the Rauisuchidae family based on a phylogenetic analysis by Lessner et al. in 2016.
facts.quote: Se considera que Vivaron es un miembro de Rauisuchidae de acuerdo con el análisis filogenético de Lessner et al., 2016

facts.statement: The presence of Vivaron in the southwestern United States, alongside Postosuchus, implies that many other rauisuchid fossils from that region previously assigned to Postosuchus kirkpatricki require morphological re-analysis.
facts.quote: La presencia de Vivaron en el suroeste de Estados Unidos, adicionándose a la de Postosuchus tiene implicaciones para la clasificación de otros varios materiales de rauisúquidos hallados en locaciones de esa área

facts.statement: The inferred close relationship between Vivaron and Teratosaurus suggests a significant biogeographic link between the Chinle Formation and high-latitude regions of Pangea during the middle Norian.
facts.quote: La relación cercana inferida entre Vivaron y Teratosaurus también tiene implicaciones para la biogeografía de Pangea a mediados del Noriense

facts.statement: Vivaron lived during the Norian stage of the Triassic, between 227.3 and 205.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Norian to Norian (227.3 to 205.7 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are three recorded fossil occurrences of Vivaron in the Paleobiology Database.
The parent group of the genus Vivaron is Rauisuchidae.
Vivaron belongs to the class Reptilia.
The type species of the genus Vivaron is Vivaron haydeni.
